analysis.one_liner: Ends the antitrust law exemption for the health and dental insurance industry.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote: it was introduced on December 19, 2018 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it stalled until the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Health insurers currently enjoy a special shield under a 1945 law, the McCarran-Ferguson Act, that generally keeps federal antitrust laws from applying to the insurance business. That shield means insurers can agree on prices, divide up markets, or merge in ways that would be illegal for almost any other industry, without fear of federal antitrust prosecution. This bill would strip that shield for health and dental insurance specifically, while carving out four narrow activities insurers say they need to keep operating: sharing historical claims data, calculating reserve adjustments, performing actuarial services, and developing standard policy forms. It would also let the Federal Trade Commission police unfair competition in health insurance even for nonprofit insurers.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who buy health and dental coverage — individuals, families, and small employers who pay premiums directly. If antitrust laws applied to health insurers the way they apply to other industries, the federal government could prosecute price-fixing, market allocation, and mergers that reduce competition, which could lower premiums and expand consumer choice. The FTC could also target unfair competitive practices by nonprofit insurers, which the current exemption largely shields.

how_it_helps.text: Declares that nothing in the McCarran-Ferguson Act modifies, impairs, or supersedes the antitrust laws with respect to the business of health insurance, including dental insurance [S2] [S3].
Lets the FTC's ban on unfair methods of competition reach the health insurance business regardless of whether the insurer operates for profit, closing a loophole for nonprofits [S2] [S3].

Keeps the antitrust shield only for narrow, technical insurance activities: sharing historical loss data, calculating loss development factors, actuarial services that do not restrain trade, and standard policy forms that insurers are not required to follow [S2] [S3].
The bill's stated purpose is to protect competition and consumers in health insurance markets [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The health and dental insurance industry, which would lose the antitrust exemption it has held since 1945 and become subject to federal competition enforcement like other industries. Insurers argue the limited sharing of claims data and standard forms that the bill would still allow is essential to pricing coverage, so they would bear both enforcement risk and the loss of industry-wide coordination they rely on.

drawbacks.text: Even the narrowed bill leaves insurers coordinating on loss data and standard policy forms, the activities critics say matter most for pricing power, so it removes less of the exemption than a full repeal would [S2] [S3].

Opponents of McCarran-Ferguson repeals generally argue that antitrust suits could raise insurers' legal costs and disrupt the data sharing and actuarial coordination insurers say they need to price coverage in volatile health markets — a cost that could ultimately be passed to consumers through premiums. This objection is not addressed in the bill text; it is the standard industry argument against such repeals.
Stripping the exemption would not by itself guarantee lower premiums; it only creates enforcement tools whose effect depends on how aggressively agencies and courts use them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — putting health insurers under the same federal antitrust rules as nearly every other business — is real but indirect, and the bill's carve-outs for data sharing and standard forms are significant concessions that keep some industry coordination legal. The main cost falls on insurers in enforcement risk and lost coordination, though industry groups would argue some of that cost lands on consumers. On balance the bill is a targeted, consumer-oriented reform, weakened by the fact that it arrived in the final two weeks of a Congress with no cosponsors and no committee action.

outcome.mechanism: A senator introduced it in the last two weeks of the Congress and it went straight to the Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended, so it simply died there.

narrative.text: Sen. Steve Daines (R-MT) introduced the Competitive Health Insurance Reform Act of 2018 on December 19, 2018 [S1] [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
The Judiciary Committee took no further action, and the bill never reached the Senate floor or received a vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health and dental insurers, who kept the antitrust exemption the bill would have taken away. Because the bill died in committee rather than losing a vote, no member ever had to record a position on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers keeping their antitrust shield

for.name: Sen. Steve Daines
for.role: U.S. Senator from Montana and the bill's only sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the Judiciary Committee; no cosponsors joined him.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred, chaired in the 115th Congress by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred, never scheduling a markup or vote, so it died when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or floor debate occurred, and the bill had a single Republican sponsor with no cosponsors from either party, so its partisan shape cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would end their exemption from federal antitrust laws, exposing pricing, market allocation, and merger decisions to FTC and Justice Department enforcement. The industry's interest in keeping the exemption runs against consumers, since the exemption removes the main legal check on coordinated pricing in a market consumers must buy into.
A companion provision would apply FTC unfair-competition rules to health insurance regardless of whether it is carried on for profit, closing a carve-out nonprofits currently enjoy [S2] [S3].

The bill explicitly preserves industry collaboration on loss data, loss development factors, actuarial services, and standard policy forms, keeping that coordination legal even as the broader exemption falls away [S2] [S3].
